Sport
sport
n. and v. (mirth made at another's expense; the entertainment the Philistines demanded of a blind Samson, and the fool's amusement in mischief)
A shortened form of disport — Old French desporter, to carry away, to divert. The Hebrew at Judges 16:25 is tsachaq, to laugh or make sport, the same verb behind the name Isaac; at Proverbs 10:23 it is sechoq, laughter.

Biblical Definition

Scripture's use of sport is almost entirely dark. At Gaza, “when their hearts were merry, that they said, Call for Samson, that he may make us sport. And they called for Samson out of the prison house; and he made them sport: and they set him between the pillars” (Judges 16:25). Three thousand watched from the roof (Judges 16:27). A blind man, shorn and grinding at a mill, was brought out as the entertainment at a feast to Dagon — and the pillars they set him between were the ones he pulled down. Proverbs names the same instinct in ordinary men: “It is as sport to a fool to do mischief: but a man of understanding hath wisdom” (Proverbs 10:23). The fool is not described as malicious but as amused; harm is his recreation. Proverbs 26:19 exposes the standard excuse: “So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?” — compared in the previous verse to a madman casting firebrands and arrows. Isaiah turns the word on the mockers of God's people: “Against whom do ye sport yourselves? against whom make ye a wide mouth, and draw out the tongue?” (Isaiah 57:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sport as play, diversion, or mirth — and also mock, contemptuous mirth, and a person made the subject of derision.

expand to see more

SPORT, n. That which diverts and makes merry; play; game; diversion.

2. Mock; mockery; contemptuous mirth. Then make sport at me. Judges 16.

3. That with which one plays, or which is driven about.

4. Play; idle jingle. An author who should introduce such a sport of words upon our stage.

SPORT, v.i. To play; to frolic; to wanton. 2. To trifle.

Key Scripture

Judges 16:25 — "And it came to pass, when their hearts were merry, that they said, Call for Samson, that he may make us sport. And they called for Samson out of the prison house; and he made them sport: and they set him between the pillars."

Judges 16:27 — "Now the house was full of men and women; and all the lords of the Philistines were there; and there were upon the roof about three thousand men and women, that beheld while Samson made sport."

Proverbs 10:23 — "It is as sport to a fool to do mischief: but a man of understanding hath wisdom."

Proverbs 26:19 — "So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?"

Modern Corruption

Cruelty framed as humour has been given a permanent excuse — I was only joking — and Proverbs 26:19 names that excuse by its own words.

expand to see more

Proverbs 26:18-19 is one of the few places where Scripture quotes the defence and answers it. A man deceives his neighbour, and when confronted says Am not I in sport? — and the Holy Ghost compares him to a madman throwing firebrands, arrows, and death. The excuse is not accepted, and the reason is that the injury is real whatever the intention was. The modern forms are familiar: it was banter, it was a joke, you are too sensitive. Where the mockery is aimed at the weak, at a wife, at a child, or at a brother in Christ, the biblical category is not humour at all. Scripture is not humourless — Elijah on Carmel is devastatingly funny at the expense of Baal — but it never permits amusement purchased with a neighbour's harm.

Judges 16:25 is the most terrible use, and it repays a careful reading of what led to it. Samson had been the strongest man in Israel and had spent his strength on riddles, feasts, women, and vengeance; he ended as a blind entertainer at a pagan festival. The Philistines were sporting with a man and, as they thought, with his God: the whole feast was a sacrifice to Dagon for delivering Samson into their hand. His last prayer asks for strength to be avenged for his two eyes, and the narrator records that the dead he slew at his death were more than they which he slew in his life. Hebrews 11 lists him among the faithful, which is a mercy the chapter itself does not explain.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsachaq, to laugh, make sport — Judges 16:25; sechoq, laughter — Proverbs 10:23; anag, to take delight, sport oneself — Isaiah 57:4.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsachaq — to laugh, mock, make sport; Judges 16:25, and the root of the name Isaac.

Hebrew sechoq — laughter, derision; Proverbs 10:23, the fool's amusement in mischief.

Hebrew anag — to be soft, to sport oneself; Isaiah 57:4, of mockers.

Hebrew zimmah — mischief, a wicked device; the object of the fool's sport.

Old French desporter, to carry away or divert — the source of English disport and sport.

Usage

"“Call for Samson, that he may make us sport” — a blind man as the feast's entertainment."

"“It is as sport to a fool to do mischief” — harm as recreation."

"“Am not I in sport?” — the excuse quoted, and refused."
